utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions concerning your examination of the documents and how you dealt with them. Now, what I want to find out firstly, when you were checking the MIIF source and MIFing, what precisely were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, for those documents that I was referring to in Annex 1 and were not retrieved on those mentioned six document missions, I was checking from the MIF record where from these particular documents were obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please expand a bit further for me specifically. Give me examples.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I found a document at OTP disposal that was not retrieved on those documents missions, meaning that I did not know exactly where it comes from, I went to this electronic MIF record or database which shows what is the origin of this particular document and how it was obtained to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What process did you use to check and determine the authenticity of a document and whether you would rely on that document for your purposes, for the purposes of your task?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, basically working in a different archives and document holdings I was using exactly same methods as historians are using. First of all, judging documents by their physical appearance, comparing it to the content of the document. Therefore, trying to find out whether the document is what it claims to be, and also corroborating information in the document with other documents or other sources that tell more or less about same things. So basically this was a process of trying to find out whether documents are reliable and whether they are authentic. I don't know whether I need to expand further my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, it would help me if you could demonstrate by reference to a particular document.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's a bit difficult to find a particular document, but, for example, documents dealing -- let's say as an example documents dealing with the Golubic training ground. And of course from the content of the document it was possible to -- to make a comparison with other documents that speak about the same training ground and through comparison to see whether the document is what it claims to be. So there's a degree of comparison when judging authenticity of documents and also physical appearance. And I must say that on those six document missions I carried out in different document holdings there was not once raised suspicion that those documents would have not been authentic or they would have been falsed or forged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm merely trying to get to the system that you employed so as to assist me in my deliberations. But in respect of an original document, how would you determine originality, and where no original is available, how would you determine whether the copy with which you are presented is the true copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as previously answered, many documents we reviewed on those document missions were copies of original documents, and of course again by judging the content of the document you can state whether document or documents are genuine. And in addition to this, in several occasions we found same document or copies of the same document in different document holdings, basically demonstrating that these are documents they claim to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to go on now to Major Knezovic -- the Major Knezovic group which you mentioned. Do you recall that? K-n-e-z-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I'm not sure which group you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Line 7 to 9. It's -- you said that they received orders, staff orders from Knin. What I wanted to know is if there was any document that confirmed or ruled out that they received staff orders from Knin.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, I didn't get the page in Annex 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Page 34, lines 7 to 9. Have you located it?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, not really. I have page 34, and I have lines from 7 to 9, but it doesn't next anything about Major Knezovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Let me go on to something else on that question. That can probably be located. This would be my last question now. Footnote number 9, part 1 of Annex 2. My apologies. There's a reference to Orsat Miljanic? Is that a person and is he connected to or an officer of the Croatian Office of Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Any questions arising from the questions by the Chamber, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, though if it's of any assistance, I think that with respect to Major Knezovic, I think he's discussed at page -- the top of page 29 of Mr. Kerkkanen's report, and I'm not sure if that's what Her Honour Judge Nosworthy was referring to in her question. I haven't been able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is there a reference to receiving staff orders from Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is -- it says: "The group -- the group seems to be act almost independently claiming that they receive their tasks directly from Knin." And there's a reference to a report there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. So what I wanted to know is whether in the course of your examination you saw any document confirming or denying the fact of receiving of staff orders from Knin. And then what I wanted to know as well, what did you understand Knin to mean in that context?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Basically there are many orders that can be regarded as staff orders coming from Knin, even from Mr. Martic himself. And by Knin, I mean orders coming from the authority in Knin, that many documents, as I have seen and we have seen, the authority is Mr. Martic or his subordinates, meaning the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kerkkanen, with regard to Judge Hoepfel's questions about the carbon copies of the documents that you found, as well as in connection with the question put to you by Honourable Judge Nosworthy, I would like to know whether you established how many documents that you analysed and provided originals and how of them many were copies? Can you tell us that? And secondly, did you have in mind that quite a lot of documents were found in Croatian archives? And we know that the Croatian interest is totally opposed to the interest of Mr. Martic, not only in this case but generally speaking, and that this different interest still exists on the side of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the second part of the question. I think it's argumentative. It's not established at all whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, regarding the second part of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it should not be disputed in this case that the Serb authorities on the one side and the Croatian authorities on the -- the other side were on the two opposite sides throughout the entire period, that they had different interests. And if documents from the Serbian archives, the alleged Serbian documents are found in the Croatian archives, this provides me with the basis for putting such a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, isn't that an issue that you can argue at the end of the case when you make your closing argument rather than argue it with the witness? Alternatively, you can ask the witness to say whether he agrees that the two were opposed and that -- and if he says yes, then that forms the basis for your argument at the close of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The meaning of my question is exactly what you have just said. Thank you for your assistance and instruction with this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, during the period that you analysed and that the documents referred to, were the Croatian side and the Serbian side in the area two sides with an entirely different, opposing interests?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what can be said from the common knowledge. And if I can continue by answering the first part of your previous question. Most of the documents we reviewed and retrieved in different document holdings, and archives were copies of the original documents, not originals. And if, Your Honour, you allow, I would continue about these archives. This documentation is part of the SAO or RSK documentation that fell in hands of Croats in 1995, and the only proper place to keep these documents are official archives where they are accessible to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more brief question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the documents were obtained by the Croatian authorities in 1995 is the explanation provided to you by the Croatian side, isn't it, Mr. Kerkkanen?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. When we were requesting access to those documents, in our request we asked if we can have access to documents obtained by the Croatian authorities in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting, I know you didn't ask the Chamber to do this, but the Chamber does remind you that you had a housekeeping issue that you wanted to raise at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate the reminder, but perhaps we could excuse the witness first because it's actually something that has to be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kerkkanen, thank you so much for coming to testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony in this case. You are now excused from further attendance. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Due to the illness of the accused in this matter, the matter is now being postponed without a date to a date to be arranged with the parties. Court adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.06 p.m.,
